rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering among God’s servants means joining the company and ranks of His sincere, righteous servants.
rows.anchor: في زمرة عبادي الصالحين المخلصين لي وانتظمي في سلكهم وكوني في جملتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering God’s Garden is the bodily happiness promised to the tranquil soul, prepared for such souls.
rows.anchor: وادخلي جنتي التي أعددتها لذوي النفوس المطمئنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first command signifies spiritual happiness through companionship with the righteous; the second signifies bodily happiness, and the superior spiritual reward is mentioned first, with the Garden completing it.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى السعادة الروحانية لكمال استئناس النفس بالجليس الصالح والأمر بدخول الجنة إشارة إلى السعادة الجسمانية

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan explains that dukhūl takes fī with a figurative or nonliteral domain, but usually takes a real container directly.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان لأن المدخول فيه إن كان غير ظرف حقيقي تعدى إليه في الاستعمال بفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes ‘return to your Lord’s promise’ as the promised Garden and company of the righteous, spoken after the reckoning; the objection that this implies prior residence is answered by a potential existence in Adam’s loins while he was in the Garden.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى موعد ربك واستظهر أن المراد بموعده تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed prior existence is compared with reports from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās that maʿād in 28:85 means Paradise rather than Mecca; this works only if Adam’s Garden was the eschatological Garden, a strongly disputed identification discussed by Ibn al-Qayyim.
rows.anchor: على ما روى عن أمير المؤمنين علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما من أن المراد بالمعاد الجنة دون مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes ‘return to your Lord’s command’ mean return to one of His affairs: His treatment of her without distress, placement in an honored station, or something similar.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى أمر ربك واستظهر أن المراد بالأمر على ذلك التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view understands the return as return to God’s general favor, from the barzakh after death or from the period after resurrection but before judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى كرامة ربك ويراد جنس كرامته سبحانه

rows.speaker: عكرمة والضحاك
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk place the address at resurrection; on one analysis nafs means the person, Lord means God, and an implied noun supplies the station to which she returns.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة والضحاك أن ذلك القول عند البعث فقيل النفس بمعنى الذات أيضاً والمراد بالرب هو الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis takes nafs as the soul and rabb as its owner, the body: the soul returns to its former body, then enters the servants and the abode of reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل النفس بمعنى الروح والمراد بالرب الصاحب وفسر بالجسد وباقي الآية على حاله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr reads ‘among My servants’ elliptically as ‘among the bodies of My servants’; singular first and plural second are compatible because the plural is generic.
rows.anchor: وجاء هذا في رواية عن ابن عباس وابن جبير ولا يضر الأفراد أولاً والجمع ثانياً

rows.speaker: ابن زيد وجماعة
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and a group say the address comes at death, with the soul understood as the spirit returning to the sacred realm and then joining the close servants.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد وجماعة إن ذلك القول عند الموت

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr reports that, after the tranquil-soul verse was recited before him, Abū Bakr called it beautiful and the Prophet said an angel would address him with it at death; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أما أن الملك سيقولها لك عند الموت

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: A similar death-time report is transmitted in al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī’s Nawādir al-uṣūl through Thābit ibn ʿAjlān and Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir from Abū Bakr; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: من طريق ثابت بن عجلان عن سليم بن عامر عن الصديق رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the death-time reading, the soul is pleased with its bliss and pleasing to God; entry among the close servants follows immediately, while entry into the eternal Garden follows at resurrection, though certainty permits the future event to follow by fa.
rows.anchor: وهذا الدخولان يعقبان الرجوع إلا أن الدخول الأول يعقبه بلا تراخ قبل يوم القيامة والثاني يعقبه بتراخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed sequencing allows both commands without delay: entry among the servants may mean joining righteous souls of one’s kind or their bodies, and Garden entry may be temporary enjoyment before the Hour.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون تعقيب الأمرين بلا تراخ إن أريد بالدخول في العباد الدخول في زمرة المقربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporary-Garden proposal cites a hadith that believers’ souls are in birds’ crops in Paradise and an athar that a believer receives half his promised Garden at death; al-Ālūsī calls the mirror-and-radiance explanation of their gathering rhetorical speculation.
rows.anchor: ففي الحديث أن أرواح المؤمنين في حواصل طيور في الجنة وفي بعض الآثار إذا مات المؤمن أعطى نصف الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ says the return is at death, meaning departure from worldly life, while the two entry commands are spoken at resurrection.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن جرير وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن أبي صالح أنه قال في الآية

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī places the address after death but before resurrection: the believer sees his Garden home, returns to the body, and awaits questioning by Munkar and Nakīr; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن المنذر عن محمد بن كعب القرظي أنه قال في الآية إن المؤمن إذا مات

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the soul is given glad tidings of Paradise at three stages: death, resurrection, and the day of gathering.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن زيد بن أسلم أنه قال في الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An inward reading applies the commands throughout earthly life: turn to God in every matter, join the sincere servants through good works, and enter the Garden potentially; al-Ālūsī says this is not a sound interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل يجوز أن يكون ذلك في سائر أوقات النفس في حياتها الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk identifies the occasion with ʿUthmān’s purchase of Biʾr Rūma for public water; al-Ālūsī treats such identifications as examples, not limits on the verse.
rows.anchor: ابن أبي حاتم من طريق جويبر عن الضحاك عن ابن عبا سأنها نزلت في عثمان بن عفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported occasions identify the tranquil soul with Ḥamza or with Khubayb ibn ʿAdī, whose face was miraculously turned toward the qibla after his captors faced it toward Medina; these too are examples.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنها نزلت في حمزة بن عبد المطلب وقيل نزلت في خبيب بن عدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to identify the soul as the Prophet; al-Ālūsī likewise treats this as an illustrative identification rather than restricting the verse’s general meaning.
rows.anchor: قول ابن عباس في تلك النفس كما أخرجه عنه ابن مردويه هو النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readings imply that souls existed before bodies in the realm of dominion; al-Ālūsī notes that most theologians, like Plato and his followers, instead hold that souls are created when bodies become ready for them.
rows.anchor: وجمهور المتكلمين على أنها مخلوقة عند استعداد الأبدان لها وكذا أفلاطون وأصحابه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك ومجاهد وأبو جعفر وأبو صالح وأبو شيخ واليماني
rows.claim: These authorities read ʿibādī in the singular, ʿabdī; al-Ālūsī takes the intended sense to be generic, as with nafs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك ومجاهد وأبو جعفر وأبو صالح وأبو شيخ واليماني في عبدي على الأفراد

rows.speaker: السادة الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufi authors see three stations in the passage—tranquil, content, and approved—and explain each in their works.
rows.anchor: وقالوا إن الآية متضمنة لمراتب ثلاث منها المطمئنة والراضية والمرضية

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Citing a teaching of the Prophet to some Companions, transmitted from Abū Umāma by al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn ʿAsākir, al-Ālūsī offers a prayer for a soul that believes in meeting God, accepts His decree, and is content with His provision.
rows.anchor: كما علم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعض الصحابة على ما أخرج للطبراني وابن عساكر عن أبي إمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubadan means abundant, from something piled together; the speaker boasts in deluded pride over believers about wealth he spent ostentatiously, calling it destruction to show he expected no return.
rows.anchor: أي كثيراً من تلبد الشيء إذا اجتمع أي يقول ذلك وقت الاغترار فخراً ومباهاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the wealth was spent in hostility toward the Messenger, with the complaint intended to injure him.
rows.anchor: وقيل يقول ذلك إظهاراً لشدة عداوته لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal sought the Prophet’s rulings on expiation after sins, then complained that obeying Muḥammad had cost him much in expiations and liabilities; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: فعن مقاتل أن الحرث بن نوفل كان إذا أذنب استفتى الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view places the boast on the Day of Judgment, when the spending proves useless and so is described as wasted wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ما تقدم أولاً إلا أن هذا القول وقت الانتقام منه وذلك يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وزيد بن علي ومجاهد وابن أبي الزنا
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads lubbadan with a doubled b; Abū Jaʿfar and Zayd ibn ʿAlī also have lubdan with a still b, while Mujāhid and Ibn Abī al-Zinād read lubadan with ḍamma on both lām and bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر لبداً بشد الباء وعنه وعن زيد بن علي لبداً بسكون الباء وقرأ مجاهد وابن أبي الزنا لبداً بضم اللام والباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether he spent to display himself or out of hostility to the Prophet, God saw and watched him, and will question and requite him.
rows.anchor: أي حين كان ينفق ما ينفق رئاء الناس أو حرصاً على معاداته صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ungraded hadith cited here says a person’s feet will not move on Judgment Day until questioned about lifespan, wealth’s source and spending, and knowledge and its use.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث «لا تزل قدما العبد يوم القيامة حتى يسأل عن أربع عن عمره فيم أفناه وعن ماله مم جمعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes ‘see’ as ‘find’ and lam as meaning lan, expressing certainty: God will find him on Judgment Day and reckon him for it.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المعنى أن لم يجده أحد على المراد بالرؤية الوجدان اللازم له ولم بمعنى لن

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the claimant lied and had spent nothing; the verse rebukes his assumption that God did not see whether he spent or not, since God knows the truth.
rows.anchor: وعن الكلبي أن هذا القائل كان كاذبا لم ينفق شيئاً فقال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder of the two eyes follows to establish God’s power to requite and account for the person, as well as His knowledge of his state.
rows.anchor: وقرر سبحانه القدرة على مجازاته ومحاسبته والإطلاع على حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the person two eyes with which to see; in context this supports the reminder that God observes and can hold him to account.
rows.anchor: يبصر بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that Thamūd denied is a fresh sentence reinforcing the failure of the soul that was corrupted in 91:10.
rows.anchor: استئناف وارد لتقرير مضمون قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes ‘successful is whoever purified it’ parenthetical after the inspiration clause, not the oath’s answer; he infers an omitted answer that God will destroy Meccan unbelievers for rejecting the Messenger as He destroyed Thamūd for rejecting Ṣāliḥ.
rows.anchor: وجعل الزمخشري قوله تعالى : { قَدْ أَفْلَحَ } الخ تابعاً لقوله تعالى : { فَأَلْهَمَهَا } الخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the objection that this requires omitting the oath’s lām and improperly emphasizing practical purification over the higher goal of certain belief.
rows.anchor: فقيل إن ذلك لما يلزم من حذف اللام وأنه لا يليق بالنظم المعجز أن يجعل أدنى الكمالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He replies that deleting the lām is common, especially after a long phrase, and is easier than deleting an entire sentence; al-Zamakhsharī himself accepts an omitted oath answer at 23:1.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكره في { قد أفلح المؤمنون } [ المرمنون : 1 ] فما حدا مما بدأ وأن التزكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification, understood as growth, is not confined to practical action and is itself an intended end, though even a prerequisite may appropriately receive emphasis.
rows.anchor: وأن التزكية مراداً بها الإنماء لا اختصاص لها وليست مقدمة بل مقصودة بالذات

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses God’s inspiration of the soul as making its course binding upon it; the report is transmitted by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim.
rows.anchor: أخرج عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Al-Daylamī also transmits this gloss from Anas as a report raised to the Prophet; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وأخرجه الديلمي عن أنس مرفوعاً

rows.speaker: الواحدي وصاحب المطلع
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī and the author of al-Muṭliʿ explain inspiration as placing guidance or abandonment in the heart; whichever God places is thereby made binding.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي وصاحب المطلع الإلهام أن يوقع في القلب التوفيق والخذلان

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn reports two men of Muzayna asking whether people’s deeds were decreed beforehand or established through prophetic teaching; the Prophet answered that they were decreed and had already passed, citing 91:7–8. The cited collections are al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and Abū Dāwūd.
rows.anchor: عن عمران بن حصين أن رجلين من مزينة أتيا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالا يا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine decree does not erase all human agency: even if God ultimately creates the acts, the servant’s participation in purification or corruption suffices for the attribution to him; the text does not prove independent power to choose and create either course.
rows.anchor: ولا يقتضي ذلك أن لا يكون لقدرة العبد واختياره مدخل في الفجور والتقوى بالكلية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the successful soul as one God purifies and guides, and the failed soul as one God corrupts and leads astray; this reading makes God the subject of the purification and corruption verbs.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال في ذلك يقول الله تعالى

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes to the Prophet the explanation that the soul God purifies succeeds and the soul deprived of good fails; it is cited through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylamī without a stated grading.
rows.anchor: أخرج عنه ابن أبي حاتم وأبو الشيخ وابن مردويه والديلمي أنه قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Arqam reports the Prophet’s prayer: asking God to grant the soul piety and purify it, since He is its best purifier, guardian, and master; cited by Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shayba, Muslim, and al-Nasāʾī.
rows.anchor: عن زيد بن أرقم قال كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ṭabarānī and others, the Prophet paused after reciting 91:9 and said the same prayer for the soul’s piety and purification.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية الطبراني وغيره عن ابن عباس أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام إذا تلا هذه الآية وقف وقال ذلك

rows.speaker: صاحب الانتصاف
rows.claim: The author of al-Intiṣāf prefers taking God as the subject of purification because the pronouns in the preceding oaths then consistently refer to God and because 87:14, with ‘purified’ as a passive-like result, fits that reading.
rows.anchor: ورجحه صاحب الانتصاف بأن الضمائر في { والسماء وما بناها } [ الشمس : 5 ]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite those reports, al-Ālūsī says the human-agent reading remains the more immediate sense; the reports do not conclusively establish the alternate subject, but refute al-Zamakhsharī’s charge that it is Sunni ‘inversion’ of the Qadari position.
rows.anchor: لا ينبغي أن ينكر أن المعنى السابق هو السابق إلى الذهن وما ذكر من الأخبار ليس نصاً في تعيين المعنى الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭaghwā is a verbal noun meaning transgression beyond the limit in disobedience; al-Kashshāf explains the wāw in the noun as a distinction from the adjective forms of yāʾ-root words, while al-Rāghib allows both wāw and yāʾ roots for ṭaghā.
rows.anchor: والطغوي مصدر من الطغيان بمعنى تجاوز الحد في العصيان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes the bāʾ as instrumental, whereas most commentators take it causally; al-Ālūsī says the difference is slight.
rows.anchor: والباء عند الجمهور للسببية أي فعلت التكذيب بسبب طغيانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further analysis makes the bāʾ attach directly to ‘denied’: Thamūd denied the torment promised by its prophet, with the punishment itself described as transgressive or excessive, like 69:5; the verbal noun intensifies without an omitted genitive.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون صلة للتكذيب على معنى كذبت بما أوعدت به في لسان نبيها من العذاب ذي الطغوى

rows.speaker: الحسن ومحمد بن كعب وحماد بن سلمة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, and Ḥammād ibn Salama read ṭughwāhā with ḍamma on ṭāʾ; it remains a verbal noun, compared with rujʿā and ḥusnā, and the wāw-root analysis removes the alleged irregularity.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ومحمد بن كعب وحماد بن سلمة طغواها بضم الطاء وهو مصدر أيضاً كالرجعى والحسنى
